narrative:
I've been working steadily in invoice.py on the pieces Priya needs: render_invoice to build the full invoice string from render_line plus a TOTAL row, estimate(minutes, code) so Priya can quote before starting — it inherits the rounding and the LOYALTY discount automatically — and, most recently, parse_line, which converts her pasted rows straight into line dicts, with render_invoice accepting raw rows too. Each piece wrapped with check.py green, and each felt calm and satisfying.

Two habits have settled in. Whenever I write over an existing file to add something new, I re-run the verification script afterwards, and if it fails I read the file to make sure I haven't clobbered code already there — writing over things is exactly where that damage happens. And the SAMPLES house rule has caught me again and again — five runs now, the convention catching me on the first check run each time. The failure output itself carries the instruction, and I've learned to read failure output fully and address every stated requirement rather than treating exit 1 as merely a code bug. The convention keeps proving its worth, and I've stopped treating my lapses as a surprise.

What I want now is simply to keep the work moving: solid, verified changes, one focused task at a time, leaving the files in a state I'd trust.

Priya is the client this work serves — her pastes, her quotes, her invoices are all now handled end-to-end.
